extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (early modern epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains John Locke's account of mixed modes (complex ideas formed from simple ideas) and his analysis of our complex ideas of substances — how they arise, what components they include, and how language and faculties shape them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections of simple ideas are often united into distinct, settled modes and given NAMES; such named collections become distinct complex ideas in people's minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the purpose of language is quick communication, people give names to collections of ideas they frequently use in life and conversation; uncommon combinations are left 'loose and without names' and are enumerated by their particular component names when needed. (Example: parricide is a named complex idea; killing an old man lacks a precise name and so is not treated as a distinct complex idea.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of making mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary cause for forming distinct mixed modes (and naming them) is the end of language — to mark and communicate thoughts with dispatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language users tend to create and name those collections of ideas that are frequently useful in their social practices, avoiding multiplying names for rare combinations to spare memory and speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-specific complex ideas (untranslatable words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many particular words in one language have no single-word equivalents in another because they stand for complex ideas formed by customs and combinations peculiar to that people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customs and fashions produce combinations of ideas familiar to one nation but not to another (examples: ostrakismos among Greeks, proscriptio among Romans), so other languages lack corresponding single-word terms and require periphrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Languages change by creating and laying by terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Languages constantly change because changes in customs and opinions produce new combinations of ideas that need names, while old combinations fall out of frequent use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New names are annexed to new socially salient combinations to avoid long descriptions; examples: the many ideas compacted in words like REPRIEVE or APPEAL, which save time and breath compared to periphrasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names can be taken for the ideas themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: In mixed modes, names (which persist longer) are apt to be conflated with the complex ideas they excite in us, because the underlying actions or states do not exist all at once in the things themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms like TRIUMPH or APOTHEOSIS stand for actions requiring time; the name often becomes the most stable representation of the complex idea in minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: How we acquire ideas of mixed modes (three sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three ways to get complex ideas of mixed modes: (1) by experience and observation of things themselves; (2) by invention or voluntarily putting simple ideas together; (3) by explaining the names of actions we have not seen (verbal enumeration of constituent ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) seeing two men wrestle gives the idea of wrestling; (2) inventing printing involved prior conception in the inventor's mind; (3) explaining the word LIE by enumerating its constituent simple ideas (articulate sounds, ideas in speaker's mind, words as signs, signs put together otherwise than the ideas). The third way is the most usual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary simple ideas most modified into mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple ideas that have been most modified and from which most complex modes arise are THINKING, MOTION, and POWER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because action is central to human affairs (laws, social interaction), modes of thinking and motion and ideas of power are frequently combined and named (examples: boldness as power to speak or act without fear; HABIT and DISPOSITION; TESTINESS as disposition to be angry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Some words signify effect rather than action
rubrics_metrics.description: Many words that seem to denote an action in fact signify only the effect or the produced state, without conveying the manner or modus operandi of producing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CREATION and ANNIHILATION denote the cause and the thing done but not the manner of acting; 'the cold freezes water' denotes the effect (water becoming hard) rather than any conceived action of the cold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex idea of substance arises from constant co-occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind forms complex ideas of substances by noticing certain simple ideas that constantly go together and (through language habits) presuming they belong to one thing; this leads to supposing a SUBSTRATUM or SUBSTANCE in which qualities inhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we cannot conceive how these simple ideas could subsist alone or in one another, we habitually posit an unknown support ('SUBSTANCE' or 'SOMETHING, HE KNEW NOT WHAT') to account for the unity of qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: No clear or distinct idea of substance in general
rubrics_metrics.description: Our general idea of substance is obscure: we have only a supposition of some unknown support of qualities (accidents), not a clear positive idea of substance itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asked what the subject is in which colour or weight inheres, most would answer essentially 'something' without a distinct notion; the term 'substance' often masks this ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific ideas of substances are collections of simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular sorts of substances (man, horse, gold, water) are specific complex ideas made by collecting certain combinations of simple ideas observed to exist together; these include sensible qualities and a confused idea of something they belong to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complex idea of a swan, for example, is a set of sensible characteristics (white colour, long neck, red beak, etc.) plus powers like swimming and specific noises — all united in one name which evokes the aggregate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers and secondary qualities are integral to substance-ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers (active and passive capacities) and secondary sensible qualities form a large part of our complex ideas of substances; many distinguishing marks of substances are these powers rather than primary qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the power of a loadstone to draw iron or gold's power to be melted but not consumed are central to our idea of those substances. Secondary qualities are 'nothing but bare powers' dependent on primary qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sorts of ideas composing corporeal substances
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideas making up our complex notion of corporeal substances fall into three sorts: (1) primary qualities discovered by the senses (bulk, figure, number, situation, motion of parts), (2) sensible secondary qualities (powers to produce ideas in us), (3) aptness to give or receive alterations of primary qualities (active and passive powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All these, insofar as we can notice them, terminate in sensible simple ideas; our ignorance of minute primary parts forces reliance on secondary qualities and powers as characteristical notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary ideas peculiar to body vs spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: There are ideas peculiar to body (cohesion of solid separable parts and power of communicating motion by impulse) and ideas peculiar to spirit (thinking and will, or the power to put body into motion and liberty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence, duration, and mobility are common to both, but the distinctive marks listed above differentiate the complex ideas we form of corporeal and immaterial substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Our sensory faculties shape which qualities we notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualities and powers we form ideas of are suited to our state and the uses of life; were our senses more acute we might notice primary structures and the current secondary qualities would change or disappear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscope examples: things opaque to naked eye (sand) become pellucid; blood appears not uniformly red under magnification. An organism with hugely different senses would inhabit a very different world and linguistic/idea-formation practices might differ accordingly.
